title: The Golden Statue and the Fiery Furnace
summary: Nebuchadnezzar sets up a huge golden statue and commands every official to bow to it at the sound of music, on pain of the furnace. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refuse, telling the king that their God is able to deliver them, but even if he does not, they will not bow. They are thrown into the furnace, a fourth figure is seen walking with them, and they come out unharmed, and the king blesses their God.
story: In chapter 2 Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of a statue whose head of gold was himself, and he confessed Daniel's God as God of gods. Now he builds a statue of gold from head to foot, as if to say that his kingdom will not give way to any other. The confession of chapter 2 has not changed his heart. The three friends, promoted at the end of chapter 2, now face the test that promotion brought. Daniel is absent from the chapter, and the text does not explain why; the focus falls on the three. Their refusal sets the pattern the book commends to every later generation under a hostile power: loyalty to the king in everything except worship.
historical:
No date is given, and the story is not tied to a known event in Nebuchadnezzar's reign. The plain of Dura was somewhere in the province of Babylon; the name, which means something like walled place, was common in Mesopotamia, and the exact site is unknown. The statue was sixty cubits high and six wide, about 90 by 9 feet (27 by 3 meters). Its narrow proportions suggest a figure on a tall pedestal or an obelisk-like pillar, and it was probably wood or another material overlaid with gold rather than solid gold. Whether it represented the king himself or his god is not said, though verse 12 links worship of the statue with serving the king's gods.

The long lists of officials and instruments have drawn scholarly attention. Several of the official titles, including satraps, are Persian words, and three of the instrument names are Greek loanwords, corresponding to the Greek kithara, psalterion, and symphonia. Those who date the book late take the Greek words as evidence of the Hellenistic period. Those who date it early note that Greek mercenaries, traders, and craftsmen were present in the Near East well before Alexander and that musical instruments often traveled with their names, and they suggest that Persian titles could reflect the language of the book's later editing.
cultural:
Public ceremonies of loyalty, in which subjects bowed before a symbol of the king or his god, bound an empire's diverse peoples together. The herald's call to "people of every nation and language" (verse 4) describes an empire that allowed local customs but required a shared act of allegiance. For most of the officials there, bowing was a civic formality and cost them nothing; many gods could be honored at once. For Jews bound by the first and second commandments, it was idolatry. That is the gap the story exposes: what looks like mere politics to the empire is worship to the faithful.

Execution by fire is attested in the ancient Near East; Jeremiah 29:22 mentions two men whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire. A kiln or furnace large enough to walk around in, with an opening from above and a door at the side, fits the brick kilns that produced Babylon's building materials. The note that the three were bound while fully clothed in robes, trousers, and turbans (verse 21) heightens the miracle: their robes were unaffected and there was no smell of fire on them (verse 27).
literary: The chapter uses heavy repetition for effect. The list of officials appears three times, the list of instruments four times, and the phrases "the golden statue" and "blazing fiery furnace" again and again, until the pomp of the empire becomes almost comic. Against that noise, the three men's answer is short and quiet (verses 16 to 18). Verse 17 can be translated in two ways. Many versions read it as a confident statement that God is able and will deliver them; the BSB takes it as a conditional, "If the God whom we serve exists", meaning if their God is as they believe. Either way the climax is verse 18: "But even if He does not". The chapter closes, like chapter 2, with the king's praise of God and his promotion of the faithful.

outline.t: The golden statue and the command to worship
The king's threat and the three men's answer
A fourth man in the fire
The king blesses their God and promotes them

doctrines.note: The empire demands worship of what it has made. The three refuse not because they are disloyal subjects but because worship belongs to God alone. Idolatry here is political as well as religious: bowing to the state's image is treated as bowing to its gods.

Their faith does not depend on the outcome. They trust God's power, but they do not make obedience conditional on rescue (verse 18). Hebrews 11:34 remembers people who by faith "quenched the raging fire".
God does not keep them out of the furnace; he meets them in it. The chapter teaches that his care for his people may come through the fire rather than around it.

words.note: Segid, to bow down or pay homage, the Aramaic word used for falling before the statue. It is related to the Arabic word for a place of prostration, masjid. The act is physical and public, which is why refusal was visible and dangerous.

Pelach, to serve, used here of serving gods, that is, of worship. The three will serve the king in government but will not serve his gods. The same word describes Daniel's service to God in 6:16 and the service all peoples give the Son of Man in 7:14.

Shezav, to deliver or rescue. The king asks what god can deliver from his hand (verse 15), and the chapter answers the question: the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, for "there is no other god who can deliver in this way" (verse 29).

Tselem, image or statue, the Aramaic counterpart of the Hebrew word used in Genesis 1 for humanity made in God's image. Nebuchadnezzar demands worship of an image he made; the faithful refuse because they already bear the image of the God who made them.

christ: The chapter shows God present with his people in suffering, a theme that finds its fullest expression in Jesus, who is called Immanuel, God with us. Isaiah had promised Israel, "When you walk through the fire, you will not be scorched" (Isaiah 43:2), and this story acts that promise out. The three men's refusal to worship an image of the emperor became a pattern for early Christians, who were pressed to offer incense to the Roman emperor and refused, and Revelation's warning against worshiping "the beast and its image" (Revelation 14:9) draws on this chapter. Whether the fourth figure in the fire was Christ himself is debated (see below), but the link the New Testament does draw is that the God who walked with the three in the furnace has come in Jesus to share human suffering and death, and to bring his people out alive.

hard.q: Who was the fourth figure in the furnace?
hard.a: Nebuchadnezzar says the fourth man looks "like a son of the gods" (verse 25), and a few verses later he says that God "has sent His angel" (verse 28). In the Aramaic, son of the gods is a pagan king's way of describing a divine being, not a title with a Christian meaning. Many Jewish and Christian interpreters therefore take the figure as an angel sent by God, as the king himself says. Many Christian interpreters, from the early church onward, have seen a preincarnate appearance of the Son of God, connecting it with other Old Testament passages where the angel of the LORD speaks as God himself. The older King James rendering, like the Son of God, encouraged that reading. The text itself leaves the identity at the level of a divine messenger; either way, the point is that God was present with his servants in the fire.

questions: For most people on the plain of Dura, bowing to the statue probably felt like a harmless civic duty. What formalities or loyalties in your world ask for more than they seem to?
"But even if He does not" is one of the Bible's great statements of faith. What would it mean for your trust in God not to depend on getting the outcome you want?
God met the three in the furnace rather than keeping them out of it. Where have you found God present in a hardship rather than removing it?
